title: Mercedes SLK R170: lower ball joint, cracked tyres and a front axle that needs sorting
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: When the lower ball joint develops play and the front tyres start cracking, a small SLK can remain drivable while ceasing to be truly safe.
content:
The front axle of an older car often betrays itself less in photos than on the road. In our case, the lower right ball joint is worn out and the front tyres are cracked. The car still moves, but the case is no longer minor in any meaningful sense.

On a SLK R170, that combination quickly removes what makes the model attractive: precision, lightness and confidence. A compact roadster forgives small play and tired rubber far less than a large saloon.

Wear that photos often hide

An advert can show a tidy shell, decent paint and an interior that still compares well. None of that guarantees the condition of the chassis. A tired ball joint does not always announce itself through a visibly sagging stance. The symptoms have to be read in motion or with the car properly lifted.

That is one of the classic limits of buying an older car that still drives. Attention goes to the engine, the roof or the body, while the basic behaviour also depends on simple, discreet but decisive parts. On a SLK, any looseness at the front is felt very quickly.

What a tired lower ball joint changes

When the lower ball joint develops play, the wheel is no longer guided with the required accuracy. The steering can feel vaguer, braking less clean and the front-end reactions harsher on rough surfaces. One loses less outright speed than simple confidence, which is often more serious on the road.

This fault should not be isolated from the overall feel of the car. A SLK R170 that feels nervous or tiring is not always suffering first from engine or gearbox issues. It may simply have a front end that no longer holds its geometry properly under load.

Cracked tyres solve nothing

Cracked front tyres are not just a visual ageing issue. They show that the rubber has aged, worked and sometimes dried out, no longer offering the safety margin that a precise convertible needs. Even if tread depth still looks acceptable, the cracking changes how much trust the tyre deserves.

The key point is not to set the two problems against each other. A new ball joint with dead tyres is not a sound base. Decent tyres fitted to an uncertain front axle will wear quickly and badly. The case has to be read as a whole, not as a sequence of small savings.

Rebuilding the front axle in the right order

The right method starts with the guiding and safety parts: ball joints, bushes, control arms or whatever the diagnosis proves to be at fault. Then come coherent tyres, followed by a full geometry setup once the play has gone. Without that order, one corrects a symptom without rebuilding the base.

Only after that does a real road test recover its meaning. On a SLK R170, the pleasure returns quickly once the front axle works cleanly again. The car becomes readable, light and calm instead of remaining a pretty shape whose every kilometre has to be negotiated.

This point completes our page on restoring the SLK 230 Kompressor. For the other issue that immediately weakens everyday use, see also our article on the SLK R170 hydraulic roof leak.
